content:
The claim that Allah began as a moon god is dealt with in the article on who Allah is, which goes through the Hazor stones, the gods of South Arabia and Hubal. This article takes a different route to the same question. It asks what the people of Mecca themselves are said to have believed about Allah, using the Quran and the early reports.

The limit is stated first. No text written by a Meccan pagan of the Prophet's time survives. What follows comes from the Quran and from Muslim reports, which a sceptic may call interested witnesses. They are the only witnesses near the time, and they are specific enough to test the moon-god thesis against.

The Quran reports the answer of its opponents more than once. "If you asked them, 'Who created the heavens and earth and subjected the sun and the moon?' they would surely say, 'Allāh'" (29:61). The same answer is given about the rain (29:63), the creation of the heavens and the earth (31:25, 43:9) and their own creation (43:87).[1]

Surah 23 has the Prophet ask three questions in a row: who owns the earth, who is Lord of the seven heavens and the great Throne, in whose hand is the dominion of all things. Each time the answer is "Allāh" (23:84-89), and each time the Quran asks why they do not take heed.[2]

Verdict: the Meccans of the Quran treat Allah as the creator and sustainer, above the sun and the moon. A god who made the moon cannot be the moon.

The Quran says that when these people were at sea, they dropped their other gods. "When they board a ship, they supplicate Allāh, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, at once they associate others with Him" (29:65). Verses 31:32 and 17:67 say the same.[3]

The point is made as a reproach, and it also describes a habit. In extremity they turned to the high God. In ordinary life they kept their lesser deities. Historians of religion know this pattern, a high God approached through lesser powers.

Verdict: the pattern reported is a supreme God and lesser powers around him. It does not describe a moon cult.

The charge against them is not that they worshipped another god in place of Allah. It is that they added to him. They set aside a share of crops and cattle for Allah and a share for "our partners", and the Quran says what was for the partners did not reach Allah, while what was for Allah reached the partners (6:136).[4] Their reasoning is stated plainly: "We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allāh in position" (39:3), and "These are our intercessors with Allāh" (10:18).[5]

The Quran replies with the theology of tawhid. Intercession is wholly His to allow (39:43-44); there is "no intercessor except after His permission" (10:3); even the angels intercede only "after Allāh has permitted" (53:26).[6] Al-Fārūqī's first principle, that God and creature are two orders and nothing stands between them, is the point of these verses.

Verdict: the quarrel was over partners and go-betweens, and it was a quarrel about Allah, not about which god to serve.

Muslim records that in the Prophet's time the polytheists circled the Kaaba saying the talbiya, "Here I am at Thy service, there is no associate with Thee." The Prophet said "Woe be upon them", because they went on to add a clause about an associate whom God has power over, in the rendering printed on quranx.com.[7]

Whatever the exact wording, the report fits the other verses. The Meccans affirmed that God has no partner as of right, then allowed lesser beings that belonged to him. The Quran calls this shirk and says that "most of them believe not in Allāh except while they associate others with Him" (12:106).[8]

Verdict: the pilgrimage cry already addressed one God, and the dispute was over what could be joined to him.

Here the Quran is hardest on them. "They attribute to Allāh daughters" (16:57); they "have attributed to Allāh partners, the jinn, ... and have fabricated for Him sons and daughters without knowledge" (6:100); and in Surah 53 it names al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt and asks, "Is the male for you and for Him the female? That, then, is an unjust division" (53:19-22).[9] Verse 53:23 calls the names "mere names you have named them, you and your forefathers".

Names, daughters and partners all stand next to Allah in these verses. None of them replaces him. A moon-god thesis needs Allah to be the moon. The Quran's own report has Allah as the Lord of the goddesses that the Meccans themselves set beside him.

Verdict: the goddesses are named as lesser beings in relation to Allah. None of them is called Allah.

The tribe of Quraysh lived by the House at Mecca. They guarded it, fed the pilgrims and sent trade caravans in winter and summer under the safety its sanctity gave them. Surah 106 turns that dependence into an argument: "Let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them, saving them from hunger, and made them safe, saving them from fear" (106:3-4).[10]

The verse does not say who the Lord of the House is. It assumes the hearers know. The Quran's own account of the House is that Abraham and Ishmael were told to purify it, and that Abraham asked to be kept "away from worshipping idols" (2:125, 14:35, 22:26).[11] On the Quran's telling, the people of Mecca kept a house that belonged to Allah and filled it with images.

A critic will say that this is the Quran's story about the Kaaba and cannot be tested by it. That is true, and the article on rites before Islam says what is known of the Kaaba from outside the Muslim sources. The claim here is narrower. The verse addresses Quraysh as people who already revered a deity of the House, and it names no moon.

Verdict: the Quran writes to Quraysh as people who honoured a Lord of the House. It argues that they should honour him alone.

The early reports name men before the Prophet who refused the Meccan rites. Bukhari records Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl refusing meat slaughtered for the idols and saying, "Allah has created the sheep and He has sent the water for it from the sky, and He has grown the grass for it from the earth; yet you slaughter it in other than the Name of Allah" (Bukhari 3826).[12] In another report he stands with his back to the Kaaba and says to Quraysh that none of them is on the religion of Abraham but he (Bukhari 3828).[13]

The name of the Prophet's father, ʿAbd Allāh, "servant of Allah", comes from Ibn Ishaq, who is a later source than the Quran. It is treated in the article on who Allah is and it fits the same picture.

Verdict: the early reports show Allah as the name of a God to whom an animal's slaughter could be owed. A moon would not be thanked for grass and rain.

The Quran does know sun and moon worship. "Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allāh, who created them" (41:37), and Abraham's search in 6:76-78 rejects the star, the moon and the sun in turn.[14] Arabia had moon gods, as the article on who Allah is lays out, and the verse shows the Quran addressing people who bowed to them. It also puts the moon among the things Allah made.

The reports above then give a test. If the Meccans had taken Allah for the moon, the verse that reports them saying Allah subjected the moon (29:61) would be absurd. They are made to distinguish the two. A critic can answer that the Quran is the only source and that it may shape what it reports. That is a fair reply, and it has one cost: a sceptic then has no evidence at all for the moon-god thesis at Mecca, only for moon gods elsewhere in Arabia.

Verdict: the thesis needs a link between the moon gods of the south and the Allah of Mecca, and the sources near Mecca point the other way. It is a polemic, not a historical finding. The rites of the Kaaba before Islam are another matter, and the article on rites before Islam takes them up without avoiding the difficulty.

The bottom line

The sources agree on a plain picture. The pagans of Mecca knew Allah as the creator and called on him in danger. They added partners and intermediaries, and the Quran's quarrel with them is over those additions. Nothing in the reports makes Allah a moon, and the Quran puts the moon among his creatures.

The question matters beyond history. The moon-god claim is used in tracts to tell Muslims that they worship a pagan idol, and to tell Christians that the name Allah belongs to a different god. The sources near Mecca describe a creator God that the pagans already named, and Arabic-speaking Christians of the region used the same word for the God of their own scripture, as the article on who Allah is shows from the Zabad inscription. A claim that the name was a moon's has to explain all of that, and it does not.

The picture comes from the Quran and from Muslim tradition, and a reader is entitled to ask for more. The inscriptions and the arguments from South Arabia are in the article on who Allah is, and the questions asked in the debate are answered in the nine questions from the floor. Allāhu aʿlam.
